items.stem: The three areas of exploration are:
items.answer: Readers, writers and texts; Time and space; Intertextuality: connecting texts
items.markingKey: Readers, writers and texts; Time and space; Intertextuality: connecting texts. They organise the course.

items.stem: "Each work belongs to only one area of exploration." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them.
items.markingKey: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an area of exploration and a course concept.
items.answer: An area of exploration is a broad organising frame for study (e.g. Time and space); a course concept is a lens (e.g. representation) applied within and across areas.
items.markingKey: An area of exploration is a broad organising frame for study (e.g. Time and space); a course concept is a lens (e.g. representation) applied within and across areas. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following two panels from a graphic novel about memory and displacement, described in words.

[Panel 1: a grandfather in a modern apartment tells a story to his granddaughter; clean lines and flat colours.]
[Panel 2: the same scene, but the apartment walls dissolve into sketchy pencil lines of a 1950s village street; the gutter between the panels has been removed, so the two images bleed into each other.]
Caption: 'He always said the village was still there, if you knew how to look.'

Discuss how this text could be used to synthesise ideas across the course, using the concept of transformation.
items.answer: Transformation: the present is transformed by memory.
items.markingKey: Transformation: the present is transformed by memory. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following meme shared on a student forum, described in words.

[Image, top: a tiny kitten stares bravely at an enormous, overflowing laundry basket. Top text: 'ME IN SEPTEMBER: I'LL START MY IA EARLY THIS YEAR'.]
[Image, bottom: the same kitten, now buried under the laundry, only its ears showing. Bottom text: 'ME, 11:58 P.M. THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DEADLINE'.]

Discuss how this text could be used to synthesise ideas across the course, using the concept of identity.
items.answer: Identity: the meme builds a shared student identity through in-group humour.
items.markingKey: Identity: the meme builds a shared student identity through in-group humour. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Language shapes what we can know."
items.answer: Language strongly shapes knowledge but does not wholly determine it – a central TOK debate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: vocabulary and framing influence perception; translation shows meaning is language-bound. Arguments against: experience and perception exist beyond language; translation and paraphrase are possible. Supported judgement: Language strongly shapes knowledge but does not wholly determine it – a central TOK debate.

The three organising areas of the course: Readers, writers and texts; Time and space; Intertextuality: connecting texts
An open, contestable question about knowledge, e.g. "To what extent does language determine what we can know?"
A record of recurring mistakes and the strategies to fix them
items.answer: An open, contestable question about knowledge, e.g. "To what extent does language determine what we can know?"
items.markingKey: C. "knowledge question" is an open, contestable question about knowledge, e.g. "To what extent does language determine what we can know?".

items.stem:
Read the following review of a film adaptation of a classic novel, from an arts website.

Three stars. The new adaptation of Jane Eyre is beautiful to look at and curiously cold to feel. Every candle-lit corridor is gorgeously framed; every gust of moorland wind arrives on cue. What is missing is Jane's voice – the furious, funny first person that makes the novel a confession rather than a costume drama. Without it, she becomes someone things happen to, rather than someone who tells us what they meant.

Explain how this text shows that meaning depends on the reader – a TOK link on language and knowledge.
items.answer: Fans of the novel agree; film lovers may value the adaptation on its own terms.
items.markingKey: Fans of the novel agree; film lovers may value the adaptation on its own terms. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.answer: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them.
items.markingKey: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a full HL mock, the Paper 1 and Paper 2 times combined are:
items.answer: 4 hours (2 h 15 + 1 h 45)
items.markingKey: 4 hours (2 h 15 + 1 h 45). HL P1 2 h 15 plus P2 1 h 45.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "A high mock result means no more revision is needed." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Results vary with texts and questions; continued practice keeps skills sharp and addresses remaining weaknesses.
items.markingKey: Results vary with texts and questions; continued practice keeps skills sharp and addresses remaining weaknesses. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a mock should be followed by reflection rather than simply a mark.
items.answer: Reflection turns the mark into specific, criterion-linked targets that guide the remaining revision. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: After a mock, a student scored P1: A 4, B 2, C 3, D 4 and P2: A 6, B 4, C 3, D 4. Identify the priority for revision and suggest two strategies.
items.answer: Analysis and evaluation (criterion B) in both papers; strategies: practise explaining effects of fewer features in depth; write comparative paragraphs analysing authorial choices with evaluation.
items.markingKey: Analysis and evaluation (criterion B) in both papers; strategies: practise explaining effects of fewer features in depth; write comparative paragraphs analysing authorial choices with evaluation.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use a narrator's voice to shape the reader's sympathies?"
Write a comparative thesis statement that answers the question.
items.answer: Model thesis: Both narrators win the reader's sympathy by addressing us directly, but Jane's confident retrospective voice ("Reader, I married him") claims control of her story, whereas Offred's fragmented, self-questioning testimony – later framed by the "Historical Notes" – makes sympathy uneasy. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Both narrators win the reader's sympathy by addressing us directly, but Jane's confident retrospective voice ("Reader, I married him") claims control of her story, whereas Offred's fragmented, self-questioning testimony – later framed by the "Historical Notes" – makes sympathy uneasy. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: A student claims: "A poor mock result predicts a poor final grade." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mocks are diagnostic; targeted revision after a mock often produces large improvements.
items.markingKey: Mocks are diagnostic; targeted revision after a mock often produces large improvements. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

Timed practice (about 65 minutes). Guiding question: How does the speaker use personal experience to challenge her audience?
Write a complete guided analysis.
items.answer: Thesis: the speaker turns a family anecdote into an accusation that leaders mistake gestures for action. (1) Precise detail (2008, forty metres, Tuvalu) gives authority and urgency. (2) Antithesis divides "you" and "we" and redefines time as loss. (3) Rejecting applause and ending on "Act." turns the audience's likely response against them. Evaluation: the confrontational stance risks alienating listeners, but its brevity makes it highly quotable for the media audience.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the speaker turns a family anecdote into an accusation that leaders mistake gestures for action. (1) Precise detail (2008, forty metres, Tuvalu) gives authority and urgency. (2) Antithesis divides "you" and "we" and redefines time as loss. (3) Rejecting applause and ending on "Act." turns the audience's likely response against them. Evaluation: the confrontational stance risks alienating listeners, but its brevity makes it highly quotable for the media audience. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

items.answer: Reflection turns the mark into specific, criterion-linked targets that guide the remaining revision.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reflection turns the mark into specific, criterion-linked targets that guide the remaining revision. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between untimed practice and practice under exam conditions.
items.answer: Exam-condition practice tests timing and recall; untimed practice develops depth and technique but can hide time-management problems.
items.markingKey: Exam-condition practice tests timing and recall; untimed practice develops depth and technique but can hide time-management problems. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write an arguable comparative thesis for the Paper 2 question: "Compare how two works you have studied use the perspective of a child or young person."
items.answer: Model thesis: Both works use a child's eyes to expose adult injustice, but Lee's retrospective narrator Scout blends innocence with adult reflection, while Satrapi's drawn child self makes naïvety visible on the page. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Both works use a child's eyes to expose adult injustice, but Lee's retrospective narrator Scout blends innocence with adult reflection, while Satrapi's drawn child self makes naïvety visible on the page. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: "Doing many full mock exams is the best way to prepare in the final weeks." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A few mocks with careful review are better than many without reflection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: builds stamina and timing; familiarity reduces anxiety. Arguments against: without feedback, repetition reinforces errors; targeted skill practice may be more efficient. Supported judgement: A few mocks with careful review are better than many without reflection. Markbands (15 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.answer: Criterion D

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

Guiding question: How does the mayor construct the library as a place of belonging?
A student's plan lists one device per paragraph. Revise it into an argument-led plan that would score higher on criterion C.
items.answer: Thesis: the mayor presents the library as a human, multilingual home rather than a store of information. (1) Code-switching in the greeting includes migrant communities. (2) Anaphora and personification contrast the phone's limits with human care (the child, the nurse). (3) The final possessive "belongs to you" transfers ownership to residents. Evaluation: the speech is inclusive but sentimental; it avoids questions of funding.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the mayor presents the library as a human, multilingual home rather than a store of information. (1) Code-switching in the greeting includes migrant communities. (2) Anaphora and personification contrast the phone's limits with human care (the child, the nurse). (3) The final possessive "belongs to you" transfers ownership to residents. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

HE'S GOT THIS.

The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.

SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!!! My cousin's friend works at a hospital and says the new phone masts in our city are making people sick. The media won't report it. Why? Follow the money. Do your own research. [18.2k shares]

Improve this weak annotation: "'Follow the money. Do your own research.' – imperative cliché." Add effect and link to purpose.
items.answer: Imperative cliché: "Follow the money. Do your own research." – familiar slogans flatter readers as independent thinkers while discouraging trust in experts.

Read the following extract from a short novel translated from Spanish (an original passage written for study).

The señora paid Rosa on Fridays, in cash, counting each note aloud as if Rosa might not know her numbers. Rosa had taught three of the señora's children to read. She said nothing. She folded the money twice and put it in her shoe, where the señora's eyes did not follow.

Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Write an arguable comparative thesis for the Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use a narrator's voice to shape the reader's sympathies?"
items.answer: Model thesis: Both narrators win the reader's sympathy by addressing us directly, but Jane's confident retrospective voice ("Reader, I married him") claims control of her story, whereas Offred's fragmented, self-questioning testimony – later framed by the "Historical Notes" – makes sympathy uneasy. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Both narrators win the reader's sympathy by addressing us directly, but Jane's confident retrospective voice ("Reader, I married him") claims control of her story, whereas Offred's fragmented, self-questioning testimony – later framed by the "Historical Notes" – makes sympathy uneasy. A strong thesis names both works, answers the question directly and states a similarity and a difference. Any suitable studied works may be credited.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Each work belongs to only one area of exploration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them.
items.markingKey: Works are often studied in one area but can be explored through all three; synthesis connects them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student's Paper 1 analyses often begin with a long summary. Suggest two targeted strategies.
items.answer: Start with a one-sentence context and thesis; practise analytical topic sentences; limit description to what supports analysis.
items.markingKey: Start with a one-sentence context and thesis; practise analytical topic sentences; limit description to what supports analysis.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Doing many full mock exams is the best way to prepare in the final weeks."
items.answer: A few mocks with careful review are better than many without reflection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: builds stamina and timing; familiarity reduces anxiety. Arguments against: without feedback, repetition reinforces errors; targeted skill practice may be more efficient. Supported judgement: A few mocks with careful review are better than many without reflection.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Language shapes what we can know."
items.answer: Language strongly shapes knowledge but does not wholly determine it – a central TOK debate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: vocabulary and framing influence perception; translation shows meaning is language-bound. Arguments against: experience and perception exist beyond language; translation and paraphrase are possible. Supported judgement: Language strongly shapes knowledge but does not wholly determine it – a central TOK debate. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following altered ("subvertised") billboard for a fictional soft drink, described in words.

[Original billboard: a smiling teenager drinks from a red can of FIZZ. Slogan: 'OPEN JOY.']
[Altered version: the word 'JOY' has been pasted over with 'DECAY' in matching lettering. A sticker beside the can reads: '35 g of sugar – that's about 9 teaspoons.' The teenager's smile has been left untouched.]

Guiding question: How does the altered billboard turn the original advertisement against itself?
A student's plan lists one device per paragraph. Revise it into an argument-led plan that would score higher on criterion C.
items.answer: Thesis: minimal alteration makes the brand speak against itself. (1) Wordplay in the slogan. (2) The concrete statistic. (3) The unchanged smile recontextualised. Evaluation: powerful but raises questions about defacing property.
items.markingKey: Thesis: minimal alteration makes the brand speak against itself. (1) Wordplay in the slogan. (2) The concrete statistic. (3) The unchanged smile recontextualised. Evaluation: powerful but raises questions about defacing property. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.
